title: Graceful Degradation
summary: Compare load-shedding policies by how they allocate unavoidable service loss across request classes.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Graceful Degradation** in *Fault Tolerance* (Vol II). By the end you should be able to:

- Compare load-shedding policies by how they allocate unavoidable service loss across request classes
- Design tiered feature degradation policies to maintain inference service availability during feature store outages
- Evaluate multi-tier model fallback cascades for graceful quality-latency trade-offs
- Justify the requirement for proactive architectural design and validation in graceful degradation systems
- Explain load shedding strategies used to protect serving availability under extreme resource saturation

blocks.source: Vol II, Fault Tolerance, § Graceful Degradation
blocks.md: During a major regional network outage, an e-commerce site suddenly loses access to its heavy, GPU-accelerated recommendation cluster. Rather than showing users empty pages or crashing, the site instantly switches to serving precomputed, generic popular items. The serving fault tolerance mechanisms developed in a later section aim to maintain full service, but graceful degradation dictates what happens when those defenses are overwhelmed.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md:
The section is organised as:

- Degradation dimensions
- Graceful degradation strategies
- Degradation monitoring and alerting

Pay attention to: Graceful degradation dimensions: quality, latency, coverage, freshness, feature completeness; Model fallback cascades (primary, secondary, tertiary, static); Tiered feature fallback (Critical, Important, Useful, Optional); Load shedding: random versus priority-based shedding, and admission control at system entry points.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain the four-tier feature degradation strategy (Critical, Important, Useful, Optional) and describe how it maintains service availability when feature store dependencies degrade.
blocks.md: The example policy blocks requests missing Critical features, substitutes validated defaults for Important features, uses cached values for Useful features, and omits Optional features. Its 5–10%, 2–5%, and less-than-2% quality-loss ranges are illustrative policy budgets, not inherent effects of those categories. Defaults and cached representations must be compatible with the model, and measured fallback quality must satisfy the chosen budget before deployment.

questions.q: A serving system under overload must drop some requests. Why does priority-based load shedding generally serve the product better than random shedding?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Both policies preserve capacity by dropping a fraction of demand, so neither inherently drops fewer requests. Random shedding ignores request value, whereas priority-based shedding turns degradation into an explicit policy that protects the most valuable traffic first. Admission control is still needed to reject work at entry, and no shedding policy guarantees every surviving request meets its target.
questions.hint: Think about: compare load-shedding policies by how they allocate unavoidable service loss across request classes.
options: Random shedding drops more total requests than priority-based shedding at the same load.
Priority-based shedding eliminates the need for admission control at the system entry point.

Random shedding treats every request as equally valuable, while priority-based shedding degrades according to a predeclared contract, serving interactive and revenue-generating requests before background or analytics work.
Priority-based shedding guarantees that no request misses its latency target during overload.

questions.q: An image classification service deploys a model cascade: ViT-Large (307M params, primary, 88% acc), EfficientNet-B4 (19M params, secondary, 83% acc), and MobileNet-V3 (5.4M params, tertiary, 75% acc). How should the serving tier execute model fallback during severe traffic spikes or partial accelerator outages?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Model fallback ladders dynamically shift traffic to lighter, lower-compute models when queue depths or tail latency violate SLAs, preserving response availability while sacrificing a bounded percentage of accuracy. Hysteresis ensures the system does not oscillate rapidly between tiers. Executing all three adds their unequal compute costs rather than reducing load. Dropping traffic violates availability goals. Converting vision models to text-only is nonsensical.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate multi-tier model fallback cascades for graceful quality-latency trade-offs.
options: It dynamically routes incoming requests to lighter secondary and tertiary models based on queue depth and p99 latency triggers with hysteresis, maintaining low latency and high availability at measured accuracy cost.
It executes all three models simultaneously on every request and votes on the majority class.
It drops all incoming traffic until additional ViT-Large GPU replicas finish provisioning.
It converts the ViT-Large model into a text-only classifier to save memory.

questions.q: Graceful degradation is an automatic emergent property of standard microservice architectures that requires no explicit pre-engineering or offline fallback validation.
questions.explanation: False. Graceful degradation requires extensive pre-engineering: fallback models must be pre-deployed or precomputed, default feature stores populated, degradation triggers (latency, error rate) instrumented, fallback accuracy validated against reduced SLOs, and hysteresis policies implemented to prevent oscillation.
questions.hint: Think about: justify the requirement for proactive architectural design and validation in graceful degradation systems.

points: You can now compare load-shedding policies by how they allocate unavoidable service loss across request classes.
You can now design tiered feature degradation policies to maintain inference service availability during feature store outages.
You can now evaluate multi-tier model fallback cascades for graceful quality-latency trade-offs.
You can now justify the requirement for proactive architectural design and validation in graceful degradation systems.
